ds-yds-2-1-mercan.metin: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. Although corals may look like plants, they are in fact animals that live in close partnership with tiny algae. The algae live inside the coral's tissues and produce food through photosynthesis, while the coral provides them with shelter. When sea temperatures rise even slightly above normal for several weeks, this partnership breaks down: the corals expel the algae and turn white, a process known as bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, but they are severely weakened, and if high temperatures continue, they may starve. Scientists are now experimenting with breeding corals that can tolerate warmer water, although they admit that such efforts cannot replace reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

ds-yds-2-1-coklu.metin: Many people are proud of their ability to multitask, believing that doing several things at once allows them to get more done. Research in psychology, however, suggests that the human brain cannot truly focus on two demanding tasks at the same time. What we call multitasking is usually rapid switching between tasks, and every switch has a cost. Each time we move our attention from one task to another, the brain needs a moment to adjust, and these small delays add up. Studies have shown that people who frequently switch between tasks make more mistakes and take longer to finish their work than those who complete one task before starting the next. Interestingly, heavy multitaskers often rate themselves as better at it than they actually are. Experts therefore recommend setting aside periods of uninterrupted time for important work and turning off unnecessary notifications.

ds-yds-2-1-cikolata.metin: Long before it became a sweet treat, chocolate was a bitter drink. The ancient peoples of Central America, including the Maya and the Aztecs, ground roasted cacao beans and mixed them with water and spices such as chilli. The drink was often consumed during religious ceremonies, and cacao beans were so valuable that the Aztecs used them as a form of money. When the Spanish brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, it was at first enjoyed mainly by the wealthy. Europeans soon began adding sugar to make the drink sweeter. It was only in the nineteenth century, with the invention of new machines, that chocolate could be produced in solid form and sold at prices that ordinary people could afford.
